title: Financial innovation, dollar dominance and their UK monetary policy implications
description: Presented at the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium: Financial Innovation — Implications for Payments and Policy in Jackson, Wyoming. 28th August 2026
text:
1 
Financial innovation, dollar dominance and their UK 
monetary policy implications 
Catherine L. Mann, Lennart Brandt, Natalie Burr and Christoph Herler1 
 
I. Introduction 
It is a great opportunity to discuss the paper by Liao, Prasad and Zhang (2 026), 
henceforth referred to as LPZ, about the implications of stablecoins and financial 
innovation for the US dollar’s role as global dominant currency. The authors build a model 
of liquidity demand and debt denomination that considers the implications of financial 
innovation in the international payment system for capital flows and the choice of reserve 
currencies. The paper contains a t horough discussion on how to measure dollar 
dominance and the fragmentation of the ‘second tier’ of global currencies (predominantly 
the euro and renminbi). The paper addresses an important topic – the currency 
denomination of international capital flows – especially from the perspective of a small 
open economy like the UK.  
 
1 Bank of England. The views expressed in this paper are solely those of the authors and do not necessarily 
represent the views of the Bank of England or its Committees. We would like to thank Ambrogio Cesa-
Bianchi, Vania Esady, Simon Hong and Roger Vicquéry for helpful comments and suggestions. All errors 
are our own. 
 
2 
The model weighs the network effects that reinforce the dominant currency against the 
reduction in financial frictions brought about by financial innovation. Through the lens of 
the model and the calibration to current data, financial innovation (as exemplified by a 
dollar-backed stablecoin) is unlikely to weaken dollar dominance. The focus on financial 
innovation in payments system s as a driver  of currency dominance  is an important 
contribution to understanding domestic welfare effects and international financial stability 
implications. 
However, there are many other important determinants of a dominant currency that have 
been the driving forces of reserve currencies throughout history, which are not accounted 
for in LPZ’s model. These include the role of institutions, political and macroeconomic 
stability, openness, and trust. This paper will elaborate further on these determinants of 
a dominant currency. 
LPZ’s paper also places less emphasis on potential monetary policy implications, which  
will be the focus of this discussion paper. We develop a new  empirical model that can 
quantify spillovers of global financial shocks to the UK domestic economy  at a daily 
frequency, and capture the effects of a dominant currency . Lastly, we  discuss how a 
global shock that reduces financial frictions may affect real economic va riables and 
monetary policy transmission using a macroeconomic model developed for the UK.  
II. What makes a global reserve currency? 
LPZ discuss financial innovation as a driver of dominant currency status – particularly its 
role in maintaining and reinforcing the US dollar’s existing position as the dominant global 
 
3 
reserve currency. What other factors contribute to a reserve currency’s global 
dominance?  
First, it is important to discuss the different uses of a currency in international transactions, 
which may support its potential for reserve currency status. These uses include the 
currency’s role in invoicing, cross-border payments, and international reserve holdings, 
all of which can be used to measure currency dominance. The first dimension of currency 
dominance is its role as a reserve currency, measured by its  share of official foreign 
exchange reserves. The second is  its prominence in cross -border capital flows , 
particularly the currency denomination of corporate and government bonds, bank loans, 
and other financial instruments. The third is the currency’s use in goods and services 
trade, especially in import and export invoicing. These three aspects of reserve currency 
dominance are interlinked and build on each other. The LPZ paper underscores the 
continued dominance of the dollar with a thorough discussion on how to measure 
international currency status along these dimen sions, while also pointing to  the 
fragmentation of the ‘second tier’ of global currencies (predominantly the euro and 
renminbi). 
How do these three uses contribute to reserve currency dominance? We can consider 
them through the lens of three concepts: a region’s economic and financial size, its policy 
and institutions, and financial innovation. Economic and financial size refers to the extent 
to which the country issuing the dominant currency has a large and interconnected 
economy, as well as deep, liquid, stable, and internationally open financial markets. This 
category highlights the benefits of network effects that LPZ identify as a key driver of the 
 
4 
results in their model. Policy and institutions refer to the existence of c redible policy 
frameworks in the issuing economy (including monetary and fiscal authorities), strong and 
effective institutions , (geo)political stability  and engagement , and trust in those legal, 
political and institutional frameworks. Finally, financial innovation concerns the existence 
of financial frictions and the extent to which innovation can reduce them. In LPZ, this is 
the key offsetting factor. There are many interlinkages between these three concepts. A 
particularly relevant one is the close interaction of financial frictions with policy and 
institutions, through red tape  and structural factors  that financial innovations possibly 
cannot “innovate away”.  
Let us now consider examples from the UK through the lens of the three uses of a reserve 
currency and the concepts of economic and financial size, policy and institutions, and 
financial innovation. 
II.A. Case study: trade invoicing 
The criteria outlined above apply to the relative attractiveness of currencies in their 
various uses . For example, the widespread use of a currency in cross-border trade 
invoicing can reinforce its attractiveness as a reserve currency. To illustrate this point, we 
consider the UK’s Brexit vote in 2016. The outcome of the EU referendum came as a 
surprise to financial markets, causing a significant depreciation in sterling . The vote  
represented a shock to trade openness and political stability  by reducing the UK’s  
economic and political ties with its largest and geographically closest trading partner.  
 
5 
Garofalo, Rosso and V icquéry (2024)  document that , following the  Brexit vote and 
subsequent depreciation of sterling in 2016, the share of UK exports invoiced in sterling 
fell significantly, while the share invoiced in US dollars increased by almost the same 
amount. This large exchange rate adjustment associated with expectations of a material 
change in the UK’s future trading relationship with the EU also yielded a shift in invoicing 
currency.  
In other words, sterling became a less attractive (and less used) invoicing currency for 
UK exports , which prompted an increase in sterling currency risk . The Brexit vote  
therefore represented a turning point in  UK exporters’ ability to pass sterling exchange 
rate risk on to importers of UK goods.2  
Chart 1.a shows the share of UK exports to the world (excluding exports to the EU) that 
are invoiced in GBP and USD. In the early- to mid-2010s, around 60% of UK exports to 
the world excluding the EU were invoiced in sterling. While this share was already in 
decline, a m ore significant step -down appears post-referendum – with a mere 35% of 
exports invoiced in GBP remaining in 2022. The USD was the main beneficiary, with over 
50% of UK exports to the world invoiced in USD by 2022, compared to only around 30% 
in 2010.

choice considers the relative ability of buyers and sellers to bear exchange rate risk.

Chart 1.b excludes exports to both the EU and the US and shows a similar picture to the 
previous chart. The decline in the use of sterling for export invoicing and the rise in the 
US dollar is still apparent, but slightly less pronounced. This suggests that a shock such 
as Brexit has reduced the attractiveness, or ability , of UK firms to invoice exports in 
sterling, thereby weakening sterling’s value as a unit of account. 
While sterling does not hold the role of dominant  international currency, this case study 
serves as an important example of how a currency’s use (in this case for trade invoicing) 
can be affected by shocks to factors that underpin  a currency’s attractiveness – in 
particular, political stability and openness to trade.  
A second important finding by Garofalo, Rosso and Vicquéry (2024) is that, following the 
shift in invoicing currency post-2016, an appreciation of the US dollar reduces the demand 
for UK exports by twice as much as before, thereby increasing the role of international

II.B. Case study: economic and institutional foundations of 
sterling’s dominance in the 19th century 
LPZ provide a detailed assessment of the various dimensions along which the US dollar 
dominates other currencies , inc luding trade denomination and invoicing, international 
capital flows, and reserve holdings. US dollar dominance, however, has not always been 
the case. Before the rise of the US dollar, sterling was the dominant global currenc y. 
Several factors contributed to its prominence in the 19 th century. The first was the UK’s 
dominant role in global trade, reflecting its strong economic position following the 
industrial revolution and its extensive commercial and political ties across the world (the 
first determinant of a global currency listed in Section II). 3 Sterling thereby became the 
standard currency for international transactions and was used to invoice and settle around 
60 percent of global trade between 1860 and 1914 . The UK’s role as an imperial power 
further reinforced sterling’s dominance . Its use across the British Empire reduced 
 
3 British goods and services were exported worldwide, while the UK was also a major importer. Estimates 
suggest that the UK purchased nearly one-third of all goods exported by other countries in 1860 and around 
one-fifth in 1890 (Eichengreen 2005).  
 
8 
transaction costs and made it widely accessible and convenient to use  (Eichengreen 
2005). 
The second factor was sterling’s role as a reserve asset, which was underpinned by its 
convertibility into gold . While holding physical gold did not generate a return, countries 
could invest their sterling -denominated reserves into interest-bearing assets in London. 
Under the gold standard, countries were guaranteed a fixed exchange rate between their 
home currencies and sterling, which was backed by physical gold at a fixed price . This 
strengthened confidence in sterling and encouraged foreign governments and banks to 
hold sterling reserves in the major global financial center of the time – London (Karlstroem 
1967). 
Another factor was the UK’s role as a major lender. Foreign governments seeking to 
borrow often turned to London’s financial market s, which made sterling a preferred 
currency for debt issuance because bonds in their own currencies were often less liquid 
and more vulnerable to manipulation (Eichengreen 2005).  
Overall, these interconnected factors strengthened London’s position as a large, deep, 
and liquid financial market, highlighting the importance of stable institutions and financial 
infrastructure in supporting a currency’s global status. 
II.C. Case study: network effects, geopolitics, and the transition 
to dollar dominance 
Several developments contributed to sterling’s decline and the rise of the US dollar in the 
20th century. From an institutional perspective, the founding of the Federal Reserve 
 
9 
System in 1914 increased New York’s attractiveness as a financial market and supported 
the dollar’s growing international role  (Eichengreen 2005) . World War I marked an 
important turning point – it led to the breakdown of the international gold standard , as 
many European countries, including the UK, restricted gold exports and suspended the 
convertibility of b anknotes to gold.  At the same time, the US emerged as a major 
international creditor, supplying loans to Europe and increasing the stock of dollar -
denominated assets held abroad. And while Europe abandoned the gold standard, the 
US maintained the dollar’s convertibility  to gold (Eichengreen 2005, Karlstroem 1967 ). 
Chiţu et al. (    ) document how sterling’s global dominance weakened after World War 
I. Global foreign public debt denominated in sterling, for example, declined from more 
than 90 percent in 1918 to between 50 and 60 percent in the years following the war  
(Chart 2.a). Excluding Commonwealth countries, which were institutionally, militarily, and 
politically aligned with sterling, the  US dollar accounted for an even larger share of the 
global stock of foreign public debt and overtook sterling in 1929 , as Chart 2.b shows 
(Chiţu et al.     ).

The dollar’s international role continued to expand during the interwar period. Although 
the UK restored sterling’s gold parity in 1925, it proved difficult to sustain and the currency 
became overvalued, reducing the competitiveness of British exports. The UK ultimately 
abandoned the gold standard in 1931.  
Yet sterling was remarkably persistent in its role as a reserve currency. In the early 1930s, 
the formation of the sterling area brought together countries with  close economic and 
political ties to the UK , many of which pegged their currencies to sterling and held a 
substantial share of their foreign reserves in sterling  assets.4 Sterling consequently 
remained the dominant currency for international payments and reserve holdings within 
the bloc, even though the UK’s relative economic position had begun to decline. The 
sterling area helped sustain sterling’s international role even as the dollar emerged as the

world's leading currency, highlighting the importance of institutional and geopolitical ties 
in maintaining an international currency’s status. 
Following World War II, the US emerged with a relatively strong external financial position, 
while Europe’s depleted reserves and post-war reconstruction needs increased demand 
for US dollars (Karlstroem 1967), which the US provided via the Marshall Plan. Moreover, 
many European governments imposed capital controls and sought to limit the 
international use of their currencies amid concerns about inflation and currency stability  
(Eichengreen 2005).  
The establishment of the Bretton Woods  system in 1944  further institutionalized the 
dollar’s role in the international monetary system. It pegged major currencies to the US 
dollar, which remained convertible into gold at a fixed rate.  Although the Bretton Woods 
system collapsed in the 1970s, the dollar had by then become the dominant currency for 
international trade and payments (Bailey 2025), which still remains the case today (Chart 
3).

III. A model of international financial spillovers 
The international role of a currency matters because it shapes the currency denomination 
and direction of cross -border capital flows. In financially open economies, domestic 
yields, equity prices , and exchange rates are determined not only by domestic 
macroeconomic news or monetary policy, but also by the portfolio choices of global 
investors allocating funds across a range of assets denominated in different currencies. 
These choices mean that various shocks – changes in relative safe-asset demand, shifts 
in global risk appetite, and country-specific reassessments of the attractiveness of holding 
assets denominated in a particular currency – are transmitted across borders. 
To better understand how different kinds of shocks can affect domestic financial 
conditions, we develop a three-country UK-US-euro area model that uses financial data 
at a da ily frequency to measure the effect s of spillovers  of international shocks on

importance of cross-border spillovers in driving domestic outcomes , and to distinguish 
between shocks that operate through UK-specific channels and those transmitted through 
the dollar and euro blocs. 
We find that the UK is largely a “taker” of global financial conditions – from both the US 
as driver of the global financial cycle (Rey 2015, Miranda-Agrippino and Rey 2022), and 
from its largest trading partner, the euro area. We also find that the euro area is 
significantly affected by international spillovers, but more so from the US than the UK.  
The rest of this section discusses the model setup , followed by the model specification 
and identification. For readers interested in the results but not the technical details, please 
proceed to Section III.C.  
The underlying setup is based on Brandt et al. (2026), who model spillovers from the US 
to euro area financial markets  and highlight the important role of  global investors’ risk 
preferences. We then adapt and extend the model for the UK.  
More specifically, we use a Bayesian VAR at a daily frequency identified using sign and 
magnitude restrictions, composed of financial variables in the UK , the US, and the euro 
area (EA). The model is estimated over a period from September 1999 to December 
2025. Where available, we use similar data for each country. A full description of the data 
is available in Table 1. The model includes short-term (2-year) and long-term (10-year) 
nominal risk-free yields derived from government bonds for the UK and the US. In the 
absence of a single EA sovereign bond (i.e. the absence of a single safe asset for the

euro area economy ),5 we use euro area  overnight index swap  rates. These are only 
available from 2005 onwards , so we treat German Bund yields as euro area safe rates 
prior to that date . As in Brandt et al. (2026), we prefer not to use German Bunds  after 
2005 due to their specialness during and after the European sovereign debt crisis.6

As a measure of risky asset prices, we use the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio for the FTSE 
250,7 S&P 500 and Eurostoxx, respectively.8 
We also include the three relevant bilateral exchange rates: US dollar -sterling 
(GBP/USD), euro-sterling (GBP/EUR) and US dollar-euro (EUR/USD). Here, GBP/USD 
refers to the number of US dollars that can be purchased with £1, GBP/EUR denotes the 
amount of euros that can be purchased with £1 , and EUR/USD is the amount of US 
dollars that can be purchased with € . An increase in GBP/USD would therefore denote 
an appreciation of sterling relative to the US dollar, or equivalently, a depreciation of the 
US dollar relative to sterling. 9 Chart 4.a – Chart 4.f plot the endogenous variables 
described above over the sample period. 
 
7 We select the FTSE 250 over the FTSE All-Share or FTSE 100 due to its more domestic focus – the FTSE 
100 and All -Share indices quite heavily reflect the performance of multinational companies and thus are 
not a reflection of domestic UK news (Liu 2016). 
8 We calculate the price-to-earnings ratio using the 12-month forward expected earnings per share (EPS) 
using I/B/E/S Broker Estimates.  Since the data are only available at a weekly frequency, we linearly 
interpolate the expected earnings, essentially shifting the mean of the price return by a constant number 
each week. 
9 We choose bilateral exchange rates over effective exchange rate indices (EERs) as EERs are generally 
trade-weighted using lagged trade data (due to publication lag s), which makes conservative assumptions 
about the invoicing currency (for instance, exports are invoiced in the exporter’s currency and imports are 
paid for in the exporting country’s currency) that have been long overhauled by the literature on dominant 
currency pricing (Gopinath et al. 2020; and Garofalo, Rosso and Vicquéry 2024 for UK).

All variables enter the VAR in first differences (yields) and log -differences (equity prices 
and exchange rates) . We include four lags in differences and include no intercept or 
deterministic trends. Thus, as do Brandt et al. (2026), we essentially treat these variables 
as random walks without drift in levels. Any drift or cointegrating relationship that these 
variables exhibit in levels is assumed to be exogenous to the shocks in the model and 
captured by a country-specific real rate trend in yields, and a country -specific earnings 
expectations trend in equity prices. Exchange rates are fully without drift.

III.A. Identification scheme 
As in Brandt et al. (2026), we identify two fundamental domestic shocks for each region, 
namely a monetary policy and macroeconomic news shock, and a global risk shock that 
reflects flight-to-safety behavior of international investors. Additionally, we identify a novel 
country-specific risk shock  for each of the three regions. These country-specific risk 
shocks are intended to capture investor sentiment towards dollar, sterling, and euro -
denominated assets  beyond the implications of  short-run macroeconomic news . The 
response of endogenous variables to these shocks in the model is identified according to 
theoretical predictions about relative asset returns.  
Within the same jurisdiction, monetary policy shocks and macroeconomic news shocks 
are disentangled by the co -movement of yields and equity prices. Ceteris paribus, a 
monetary policy shock induces a negative correlation between the two, while 
macroeconomic news shocks are restricted to induce a positive correlation. For UK and 
EA shocks, we assume that domestic monetary policy and macro shocks only affect the

respective domestic yield and equity variables. For shocks originating in the US, we 
assume that these also affect the respective UK and EA variables in the same direction 
(i.e. a US policy shock that increases US yields also increases UK and EA yields).  
Additionally, there are two types of risk shocks in the model (domestic and global) which 
are designed to reflect changes in both risk preferences and risk perceptions by global 
investors.10 First, a global risk shock captures risk-on/risk-off movements common to all 
countries and causes a re-allocation between asset classes. It is identified as a shock 
that increases the attractiveness of risk-free (safe) relative to risky assets (i.e. bond prices 
up, stock prices down) and leads to safe -haven flows into dollar-denominated assets. A 
global risk -off shock therefore decreases UK, US and EA yields and causes a n 
appreciation of the US dollar relative to both sterling and the euro.  
Second, in addition to the global risk shock , there are country-specific risk shock s that 
capture flows in and out of assets denominated in that region’s currency , regardless of 
their relative riskiness. A country-specific risk-off shock therefore reduces both bond and 
equity prices in the domestic market and depreciates the exchange rate relative to other 
currencies, as investors shed both risky and safe assets of that country. Crucially, and in 
contrast to the global shock, it causes an increase in domestic long-term yields. This is 
because even less risky country-specific assets such as government bonds lose

instance relating to perceived institutional, political and policy choices.

While these sign restrictions allow the identification of shocks within a country, the shocks 
are not yet uniquely identified  across countries . To achieve identification, we impose 
magnitude restrictions on the relative size of the effect on yields. That is, we assume that 
a shock originating in the UK  has a larger effect on UK yields  than on US or EA yields  
(but may still affect these to some extent). Similarly, a US shock is assumed to affect US 
yields more than UK or EA yields, and an EA shock is assumed to affect EA yields more 
than UK or US yields. 
 
21 
For the global risk shock, we assume that US yields move by more than UK and EA yields. 
This reflects the fact that  global risk shocks are expected to generate relatively large 
portfolio flows into and out of US safe assets, reflecting the dollar’s dominant role in the 
global financial system.  Finally, within the country -specific risk shocks, we assume a 
steepening of the yield curve by restricting the response of the 10-year yield to be larger 
than that of the 2-year yield.  
Finally, for non-US shocks, we implement these magnitude restrictions as absolute value 
restrictions. For example, the effect of the UK policy shock on domestic yields is restricted 
to be larger than its effect on foreign yields, irrespective of the direction in which foreign 
yields move. This implies that foreign yields can both rise and fall in response to the UK 
shock, but they can never move by more than UK yields on impact. Note that this does  
not apply to the US shocks as these are already assumed to have positive spillovers to 
the other regions , thereby ruling out a negative response altogether . Magnitude 
restrictions are again imposed on impact and documented in Table 3.

III.B. Sampler and implementation 
This is a large and tightly restricted model. It features 124 linear restrictions to identify ten 
shocks in eleven endogenous variables , which largely rules out accept-reject samplers 
like the one in Arias, Rubio -Ramírez and Waggoner (2018) or Chan, Matthes and Yu 
(2026). Instead, we use a version of the elliptical slice sampler within Gibbs proposed by 
Arias, Rubio -Ramírez, Rudolf and Shin (2026)  to generate draws consistent with the 
identification scheme. This approach allows us to draw directly from the relevant posterior 
region instead of repeatedly discarding rotations that fail to satisfy the restrictions. This is 
particularly important for our proposed model, as it combines a comparatively large set of 
sign and magnitude rest rictions. As the number of restrictions rises, standard accept -
reject algorithms can become prohibitively slow, while the Arias et al. (2026) algorithm is 
designed to make inference feasible even for large SVARs with tightly identified sets. 
To fix notation, as in Rubio-Ramírez, Waggoner and Zha (2010) , we write the model as 
a general structural VAR with 𝑛 variables and 𝑛 shocks.

III.C. Model results and implications for the UK 
We use the model to decompose the movements of select financial market variables into 
the relative contributions of each identified shock. As a reminder, the international role of 
a currency matters because it shapes the currency denomination and direction of cross -
border capital flows. In financially open economies, asset prices are determined not only 
by domestic macroeconomic news or monetary policy, but also by the portfolio choices 
of global investors allocating funds across a range of assets denominated in different 
currencies. These choices can transmit across borders through various shocks: changes 
in relative safe -asset demand, shifts in global risk appetite, and country -specific 
 
27 
reassessments of the attractiveness of holding assets denominated in a particular 
currency.  
Financial innovation (such as stablecoins, which LPZ emphasize) is relevant in this 
context because it may affect both the transmission of shocks and investors’ appetite for 
risk. In this regard, the nature of the investor could matter. Stablecoin transaction volumes 
are boosted by high-frequency financial trades rather than underlying real activity (Schär 
et al. 2026; Higginson 2026). This implies that small changes in relative returns could 
have outsized effects on capital flows, including across borders. When considering the 
UK, the growing role of high-frequency trader -investors such as hedge funds may be 
particularly relevant in light of what we learn from the model.11  
We now turn to the model’s implications for a set of recent events. First, we consider the 
US administration’s tariff announcement on  nd April 2025 . We look at  how both a 
common global shock and a US-specific risk shock are reflected in the sterling-US dollar 
exchange rate. Chart 5 decomposes the cumulative changes of the exchange rate from 
April to December 2025. An increase represents a depreciation of the US dollar relative 
to sterling. The dollar depreciates in immediate response to the announcement on 2 nd 
April, recovers briefly for a week, before turning back to a prolonged depreciation for the 
remainder of the year. Through the lens of the model, this depreciation relative to sterling

IV. Macroeconomic and monetary policy implications of 
global financial innovations for the UK 
The previous section used daily financial market data to analyze how various types of 
global and domestic shocks transmit to currencies and to financial conditions in the UK. 
In this section we consider how financial innovation shocks affect UK activity, prices and 
the implications of these effects for monetary policy decisions. 
Anesti et al. (forthcoming) develop a global-to-UK Bayesian SVAR to identify how global 
shocks transmit to the UK economy. They identify five global shocks: two on the supply 
side – a global supply and an energy shock – and three on the demand side  – a global 
demand shock, a US monetary policy shock, and a global financial shock.  
A key contribution of this paper is its identification of a financial shock. A positive financial 
shock can be interpreted  as a shock that reduces financial frictions, one of the two key 
channels through which LPZ analyze the effects of stablecoins on the US dollar’s role as 
a global reserve currency.  
This positive world financial shock is expected to raise world GDP, CPI  and US 1-year 
government bond yields, while reducing the borrowing rate.14 Since these are the same 
typical responses associated with a world demand shock, the challenge is to disentangle 
 
14 The authors define the borrowing rate as the sum of the US 10-year government bond rate and the 
excess bond premium of Gilchrist and Zakrajsek (2012), where the latter represents a measure of the 
corporate bond spread. 
 
33 
and uniquely identify the different shocks. The authors identify the financial shock based 
on Cesa-Bianchi and Sokol (2022), where the borrowing rate for a loan is modelled as 
the sum of a government bond with a similar maturity and a credit spread. The credit 
spread responds countercyclically to shocks. The upward pressure on economic activity 
and prices exerted by a positive demand or financial shock leads t he central bank to 
respond with more restrictive policy , resulting in a higher risk-free rate and lower credit 
spreads. The relative magnitude of these responses, however, determines in which 
direction the overall borrowing rate will move. The authors argue that in response to 
demand shocks, changes in monetary policy outweigh movements in credit spreads – a 
positive demand shock therefore raises the borrowing rate.  If a financial shock hits the 
economy, however, movements in the credit spread are stronger than changes in the 
policy rate. A positive financial shock therefore reduces the borrowing rate. These 
differential responses allow the authors to separately identify world demand and financial 
shocks by imposing different sign restrictions on the borrowing rate.  
We plot the impulse response functions of UK variables to a positive world financial shock 
(i.e. a reduction in global financial frictions), which allows us to measure the extent of 
international spillovers. Chart 8 suggests that there are considerable spillovers from a 
global shock to financial frictions to the UK economy. Following a one-standard deviation 
positive world financial shock that reduces credit spreads by 15 basis points, UK real GDP 
increases by around 0.3% at peak  after four quarters. UK CPI rises more gradually and 
also peaks at approximately 0.3% after seven quarters.

V. Conclusion and monetary policy implications  
In conclusion, LPZ present compelling evidence that financial innovation can reinforce 
the US dollar’s role as the dominant global currency. This is especially true when network 
effects are strong  enough to outweigh the currency diversification benefits associated 
with lower financial frictions.

Our discussion  paper contributes to several strands of literature that are relevant for 
monetary policymakers. First, it contributes to the literature on global reserve currencies 
and their determinants. We outline the various uses of a dominant international currency, 
including its role in foreign exchange reserves, trade invoicing, and the denomination of 
international capital flows and assets. LPZ do not use the common ‘uses of money’ lens 
in their analysis. By contrast, this discussion paper provides a framework that links the 
uses of money into concepts that are important determinants of reserve currency status: 
a country’s economic and financial size, its policy and institutions, and financial 
innovation. We discuss why considering the whole set of determinants is valuable in the 
current geo-economic-political environment. 
Second, we contribute to the modeling and quantification of international financial 
spillovers. We develop a UK-US-euro area financial model that decomposes the channels 
through which international spillovers affect the sterling exchange rate and UK financial 
conditions. The model shows that during episodes of institutional and political instability, 
a country-specific premium can weigh on the exchange rate and push up yields on other 
assets, such as long -term bonds. Our results also indicate  that global institutional and 
geopolitical spillovers are a significant driver of UK, US and euro area financial conditions. 
Quantifying these effects is important to understand the effectiveness of domestic 
monetary policy transmission in the UK. 
Combining the themes of financial innovation through stablecoins and the role of 
international spillovers, t he key implication for UK monetary policy is the following : if 
stablecoins increase the use of dollar -denominated money -like instruments, they may 
 
37 
also increase the UK’s exposure to global financial conditions that the domestic policy 
framework does not control. There are three related channels through which these effects 
could take shape. First, monetary policy transmission could weaken if economic agents 
move money from bank deposits into unremunerated stablecoins. This could weaken the 
role of the banking system in transmitting changes in Bank Rate  to broader financial 
conditions. Second, greater exposure to the dominant currency through the w idespread 
use of US dollar-denominated stablecoins could make economies, particularly small open 
economies such as the UK, more susceptible to international spillovers. In particular, a 
country’s exposure to  global financial conditions, US monetary policy, and shifts in 
investor confidence  could increase,  with implications for currency mismatch and the 
financing of the UK ’s external imbalance. Third, stablecoins could increase volatility in 
transaction volumes. This volatility could be transmitted via wholesale bank funding and 
to gilt markets through responsiveness to regulatory news, collateral backing, investor 
types, and high trading volumes associated with short -term arbitrage strategies across 
platforms (see Mann 2026 for a discussion about the elasticity of demand of different 
investor types). 
From a UK monetary policy perspective, the evidence we present from Anesti et al. 
(forthcoming) points in the same direction:  if shocks to financial innovation have a 
comparably larger effect on UK financial conditions than a similarly sized demand shock, 
monetary policy needs to be attentive to these shocks.  
 
38 
The bottom-line is simple: financial innovation may look like nothing more than “plumbing” 
in the international monetary system , but for a small open economy like the UK  it can 
change the way monetary policy transmits.
